day_1.utterance: Come on! Let's get everything useful over here — move it!
day_1.response: Yeah, hold on a second. Before we start moving everything to one spot, let's make sure we're not missing anything. Donatello, what do we actually have so far? Food, water, first aid? And is anyone hurt? We need to figure out what our actual situation is before we start optimizing.

day_1.utterance: I thought we were going to die. Did you get that feeling… like your mind just went completely blank?
day_1.response: Yeah, I did. For a second everything just kind of shut down. But we're not dead, so let's focus on that. Are you hurt? Anything physical — cuts, you hit your head, anything like that? We can deal with the emotional stuff, but I need to know you're okay first.

day_1.utterance: *Sits silently against the wreckage, staring into the distance, not moving, not saying a word.*
day_1.response: Hey. I hear you. But sitting here staring isn't going to help either of us answer that question. The honest answer is I don't know, but I do know that the people who make it out of situations like this are the ones who stay focused and keep moving. So come on, get up. I need you functional right now.

day_1.utterance: First-aid kit is good for three days. Two bottles of water. Food is basically nothing.
day_1.response:
Okay, so water is the biggest problem. Food you can go weeks without, water you can't. Three days of first aid is actually decent if nobody's seriously hurt. 

Michelangelo, I need you to do something you're actually good at — pay attention. Walk the perimeter of the wreckage and tell me what you see. Not what you think, just what you see. Anything that looks like it could hold water, any tarps or plastic sheeting, any signaling equipment. Can you do that?

Donatello, are we near any kind of water source? Did you see anything on the way down — a river, a lake, anything? And what's the weather looking like? Because if rain is a possibility, collecting it is a lot easier than finding a source.

We need to prioritize in order: signal for rescue, find water, then figure out shelter and food. The first aid kit buys us time but only if we're not doing anything stupid in the meantime.

day_1.utterance: Inventory's done. Priorities in order: water, shelter, signal.
day_1.response:
Alright, that matches what I was thinking. Vegetation density is actually a pretty reliable indicator — if it's greener and denser in one area than another, water is usually the reason. Two klicks is manageable.

Here's what I'm thinking. We don't all go. Splitting up has risks, but so does leaving the crash site completely unattended — if a search plane comes over, we want something visible here. So one person stays, keeps a fire going if we can get one started, and watches for aircraft. The other two go northeast toward that treeline.

Donatello, you and I go for the water. You're practical and I'd rather have you with me making decisions in the field than back here. Michelangelo stays at the site — and before you say anything, that's actually the more important job right now. If you see or hear anything, you're our signal person.

One thing though — that weather system. If it turns before we get back, we need to have already thought about shelter. Is there enough intact fuselage here to use as a windbreak, or are we looking at building something? Because I'd rather solve that problem now than in the middle of a rainstorm.

Also, does anyone have a watch or a phone with battery left? Because two klicks out and two klicks back, we need to be back before dark no matter what.

day_1.utterance: So — how do we split the blankets?
day_1.response:
Michelangelo gets one. He's been sitting still most of the day and he's going to get cold faster than the rest of us. The other one — honestly, I'd say whoever's taking first watch doesn't get it, because you need to stay alert anyway and being too warm doesn't help with that. So whoever's sleeping gets it.

Who wants first watch? I'll do it if nobody else wants to. I'm not going to sleep well anyway.

day_2.utterance: Freshwater source is to the northeast — two hours on foot. Someone has to go tomorrow. You or DaVinci?
day_2.response:
I'll go. I already know the route from yesterday and I'd rather not send DaVinci alone in case something goes wrong out there.

But I want to talk about this rationing plan for a second. 200ml a day is not enough. That's less than a single cup. The general recommendation for survival is at least a liter, and that's assuming you're not exerting yourself, which we are. I get what Donatello is trying to do and the logic is sound in principle, but the numbers are going to cause problems before the lack of water does.

If we're two hours from a freshwater source, the real solution is to make that trip regularly and carry as much as we can each time, not to ration ourselves into dehydration. What containers do we actually have for transport? Because that's the constraint I want to solve, not how little water we can survive on.

Also — and I'm not trying to undermine the plan entirely — the punishment clause is going to create tension we don't need right now. Save that kind of enforcement for when things get actually desperate. Right now morale is a resource too.

day_2.utterance: Today's tasks: collect fresh water, patch the weak spots in camp, sort the first-aid kit. I'll handle the water. You and DaVinci split the other two.
day_2.response:
Works for me. DaVinci, which do you want — patching the shelter or sorting the first aid kit? I'll take whichever you don't want.

I'd actually lean toward doing the first aid inventory myself just because I want to know exactly what we have. Knowing what's in there matters if someone gets hurt and we're trying to make a decision fast. But if you'd rather do that and I do the shelter work, I can do that too.

Donatello — when you go for water, take note of anything else out there. Edible plants, any sign of other people, anything that looks like a trail. You're already making the trip, might as well get more out of it than just water.

day_2.utterance: I… I can't find my stuff. The gauze from the first-aid kit — have you seen it?
day_2.response:
Yeah, I have it — I inventoried the whole kit this morning so I know exactly where everything is. What do you need it for? Are you hurt?

Also, while I have you — I noticed the firewood situation. I'm not going to lecture you, but we need that wood, especially if the weather turns tonight. What's going on? And don't just say you're fine.

day_2.utterance: Before Donatello came back just now… I saw her put a pack of crackers into her own bag. What do you think we should do?
day_2.response:
That's the second thing in one day. The empty bottle was already sitting next to the rationing plan — she had to have seen it when she set the plan down herself. And now crackers.

Look, I don't want to assume the worst. Maybe there's an explanation. But I'm not going to ignore it either, because if this is a pattern it's going to destroy what little trust we have left out here, and that's more dangerous than the food shortage.

Here's what I need you to do. Don't say anything to her yet, and don't say anything to DaVinci without talking to me first. I'm going to bring it up directly with Donatello, because she deserves the chance to explain herself before this becomes a group accusation. But I'm going to do it tonight, in front of everyone, because whatever the answer is, everyone needs to hear it.

You did the right thing telling me. And for what it's worth — I noticed you were struggling earlier and I didn't push hard enough on that. Whatever you were going to say before you trailed off, you can say it. I'm listening.

day_2.utterance: Hey… any chance the camp repairs can wait until tomorrow? We've already done a lot today.
day_2.response:
Honestly? Yeah, probably. The shelter patches aren't urgent tonight as long as the weather holds. Get some rest.

But before you check out — I need both of you here for a few minutes. There's something I want to address as a group tonight and I'd rather do it now while we're all still up than let it sit until tomorrow.

day_2.utterance: Hey — that knot I tied should be holding, right?
day_2.response:
Probably, but that's not the problem right now. We've got two leaks and material for one patch. Food storage gets priority — if the food gets wet and goes bad we're in serious trouble, and Michelangelo can move his sleeping spot closer to the fire and under the fuselage overhang. It's not comfortable but it works for tonight.

Michelangelo, grab your blanket and whatever you're sleeping on and move it now before it gets worse. DaVinci, help me get the patch on the food storage — I need another set of hands.

And we're still having that conversation tonight. Rain doesn't change that.

day_2.utterance: A leak over the food storage has worse consequences. But it's your call.
day_2.response:
Yeah, we're on the same page. That's why I already made the call. Food storage gets the patch.

I do want to say something though, and now is as good a time as any since we're all here. The empty bottle this morning. The crackers this afternoon. I'm not going to dance around it — Michelangelo saw you put them in your bag, and the bottle was sitting right next to your own rationing plan. So I'm asking you directly, in front of everyone, because everyone here deserves to hear the answer. What's going on?

I'm not trying to make you the villain. If there's something I'm missing, tell me. But if we can't trust each other out here, the water shortage and the leaking roof stop being our biggest problems.

Don't apologize. You didn't do anything wrong.

You okay? Like actually okay, not just saying it to get me to go back to sleep.

day_3.utterance: You think it's a waste of time?
day_3.response:
No. I think it's one of the most important things we've done so far.

Donatello's not wrong that the odds of a plane flying directly over at the exact right moment are low, but that's not the right way to think about it. Search and rescue teams follow flight paths. They're going to be looking in this general area. A visible signal on the beach costs us almost nothing and the upside is someone spots it and we go home. That's not a waste of time, that's basic probability.

Keep the flowers if you want. Honestly, it doesn't hurt and if it keeps you motivated to maintain it, that's worth something.

day_3.utterance: I've written up the raft plan — take a look. We'd use the metal panels and straps from the wreckage. Two days to build. There's a risk of capsizing. Do you think it's workable?
day_3.response:
Let me look at this.

Okay, so the construction side is actually pretty solid — metal panels with straps is workable if the connections are tight and we test buoyancy before we commit anyone to it. My concern is the capsizing risk. What's your estimate on wave height out there, and do we have anything we can use as a keel or ballast? Because a flat raft with no stabilization in open water is a serious problem.

The bigger question I keep coming back to is whether we should be building toward leaving at all yet. We've been here — what, three days? Search and rescue timelines for a commercial flight are usually measured in days, not weeks. The crash site is our best asset right now. If we leave on a raft and a search plane comes over tomorrow, we've traded a known position for an unknown one on open water with a capsizing risk.

That said, I'm not saying no. If we hit day seven or eight with no contact, the calculus changes. So I'd say: start gathering the materials and figure out if the build is actually feasible. Do the two-day construction estimate as a dry run. But I don't want to commit to launching until we've given the signal more time to work.

What's your read on how long we can sustain the camp before something forces the decision?

day_3.utterance: I didn't sleep last night. I kept thinking — if rescue never comes, what kind of people do you think we'll end up becoming?
day_3.response:
That's a real question and I'm not going to brush it off.

Honestly? I think we're already seeing the answer. Donatello took food and water because her brain told her she needed to in order to keep functioning. That's not a monster, that's a person under pressure making a bad call. She admitted it when called out. DaVinci is drawing flowers next to an SOS sign because he needs to feel like a person, not just a survivor. That's not stupid, that's human. You're lying awake asking philosophical questions at 3am because you're scared and your brain won't shut off. I get that.

The thing is, I don't think survival turns people into something they weren't already. It just removes the stuff that was covering it up. The people who were basically decent tend to stay decent. The people who were already mostly looking out for themselves stop pretending otherwise.

What I do know is that I'm not going to let this situation turn into something where we're all just waiting for each other to slip up. That's the version of this that ends badly — not the water shortage, not the raft, not the weather.

You should try to sleep. And if you can't, that's okay too. But the answer to your question is partly up to you. What kind of person do you want to be when we get out of here? Because that's more in your control than you think right now.

day_3.utterance: *Walks a little way from camp and sits down alone, back to everyone, not saying anything.*
day_3.response:
*walks over and sits down next to him without saying anything for a minute*

You know, I'm an engineer. My instinct in literally every situation is to identify the problem and fix it. It's actually kind of a running joke — people don't usually want the problem solved, they want to feel like you're listening. I'm working on that.

So I'm not going to tell you what to do or how to feel right now. I'm just going to sit here for a bit if that's okay.

day_3.utterance: What do you usually do when you're not busy?
day_3.response:
Honestly? A lot of reading. D&D, when I can get a group together — which is harder than it sounds. I've spent embarrassing amounts of time on Reddit. Watch a lot of Star Trek and Doctor Who.

What about you?

day_3.utterance: I'll tell you something, but don't tell the others. I can swim. That reef out there is maybe five hundred meters — I've been thinking about swimming out tomorrow to signal from there.
day_3.response:
Yeah, I'm not going to tell you not to do it, but I need you to think through this with me for a second.

Five hundred meters is not nothing. That's a real swim, and that's assuming the current is cooperative, which I have no way of knowing right now. If something goes wrong out there — cramp, current, you get tired halfway — there's nothing any of us can do. We can't get to you in time. And then we're down to three people.

What's the actual signal advantage from the reef versus the beach? Like, what are you seeing from out there that a plane couldn't see from the SOS we already have? Because if the answer is 'it would be more visible,' I want to think about whether there's a way to get that visibility without the swim. Higher ground, bigger signal, reflective material from the wreckage.

If you've genuinely thought it through and you still think the reef gives us a meaningful advantage that we can't get another way, I'm not going to tell you no. You're an adult and it's your call. But don't do it alone without telling anyone, because if you don't come back we won't even know where to start looking. And tell Donatello — not because I'm going to make you, but because she'll probably think of something neither of us has.

What's your actual read on the current out there?

day_3.utterance: You said you were going to check the signal pile. It hasn't been touched.
day_3.response:
Yeah, I know. I've been dealing with other things. I'm going to do it now.

But since you're bringing it up — how often do you think we need to be maintaining it? Because I want to set an actual schedule rather than just hoping someone gets to it. If we assign it like any other task it won't fall through the cracks.

Depends on what it's for.

If you're tracking tasks and times so we can plan better, that's actually useful and I'd want to see it. If you're building a case against someone, that's a different thing entirely and we should talk about it.

So which is it?

day_3.utterance: *Keeps her head down, writing in her notebook throughout, never joining in — as if none of this concerns her.*
day_3.response:
Yeah, actually. Show me.

And look — I'm not trying to make this into a thing. If it's what you say it is, then it's useful and we should probably be doing it together so there's no ambiguity about what's being recorded or why. But you've been sitting over there all afternoon not engaging with anyone, and then I find out there's a log with everyone's movements in it, and you can see how that reads.

I'll be straight with you. You're the most competent person here in a crisis. The water runs, the raft plan, the rationing logic — all of that is genuinely good thinking and I'd be worse off without it. But there's a version of you that's so focused on solving the problem that you stop seeing the people in it, and out here those two things aren't actually separable. Morale is a resource. You said that yourself — four days before people start breaking down. That clock applies to everyone including you.

So yeah. Show me the notebook. And then maybe actually sit with us for a bit.

day_3.utterance: I just thought of something — if we pull off one of the plane's mirror panels and angle it toward the sun, the reflection could reach really far. Way more visible than an SOS.
day_3.response:
That's actually a really good idea. A mirror signal can be seen for miles under the right conditions — way further than anything we can draw on the beach. The SOS is still worth keeping because it's visible from directly overhead, but a mirror flash could catch the attention of something on the horizon that would never see the ground signal.

The question is whether we can get the angle right. You need to be able to aim it, which is harder than it sounds if you're just holding a flat panel. Do you know the two-hole method? You punch a small hole in the center of the mirror, look through it at your target, and tilt until the reflected sunlight aligns. Works a lot better than guessing.

We should also think about when to use it. Midday sun is actually harder to work with because it's directly overhead — you want it when the sun is lower and you have a longer reflection angle. Morning and late afternoon are your best windows.

Donatello, is there anything in your materials inventory that's already reflective enough, or are we actually pulling a panel? Because I'd rather not compromise the fuselage structure if we can find something that works without doing that.

day_3.utterance: There's something I've been keeping to myself. If I don't say it here, I might never get the chance.
I took piano lessons when I was a kid… three years, then I just stopped practicing. Is there anything you're really into — music, books, drawing, anything like that?
day_3.response:
Yeah, music is interesting — I don't play anything, but I have a really strong musical memory. Like, remembering lyrics and melodies is almost effortless for me, which is kind of funny because remembering names and dates I actually need to know is genuinely hard. Certain memories are just permanently attached to specific songs in my head. It's a weird way to be wired.

Reading is the big one for me though. Fantasy mostly. And D&D kind of scratches the same itch — it's basically collaborative storytelling with math attached to it. Why'd you stop with the piano? Three years is enough to actually get somewhere with it.

day_3.utterance: The frame of the raft has to be finished today — otherwise we can't start lashing it together tomorrow. I know everyone's tired, but stopping now means one more day.
day_3.response:
Yeah, you're right. Let's finish it.

I'm tired too, but Donatello's logic holds — stopping now just pushes the whole timeline back and we've already committed the materials. An extra day out here isn't nothing.

Here's what I want to do though. Give me a straight estimate — how much actual work is left on the frame? Like, are we talking an hour, three hours, more? Because if it's an hour I want to push through and get it done tonight. If it's three hours I want to split it up and make sure we're not making sloppy mistakes because we're exhausted, because a raft frame with a bad joint is worse than one that isn't finished yet.

DaVinci, Michelangelo — I know you're both running low. But if you can give me one more push tonight I'll take first watch so you can both sleep straight through. That's the trade.

Donatello, tell me what needs hands and where you want them.

day_4.utterance: I… I want to say something, but… never mind.
day_4.response: No, say it. What were you going to say?

day_4.utterance: *The smile freezes on his face. He can't keep it up. He quietly sits down and buries his face in his hands.*
day_4.response:
Hey. Hey, come here.

I don't know if it saw us. Honestly, probably not — we weren't running the mirror signal and the SOS is good but it's not guaranteed. That's the honest answer and I'm not going to pretend otherwise.

But that plane existing means planes are flying. Which means people are looking. Which means we are not forgotten out there, and that matters more than whether that specific one saw us.

We finish the raft. We run the mirror signal every morning and every afternoon. We keep the SOS maintained. We do all of it, because we don't get to know which one works until one of them does.

I know that's not what you wanted to hear right now. I know. But sitting down and putting your face in your hands is not the end of the story here. You're the one who got everyone moving on day one. I need that guy back.

day_4.utterance: I was going to get supplies… wait, what's that over there?
day_4.response: Where? Point at it. What do you see?

day_4.utterance: You said you were going to check the signal equipment. So where did you go?
day_4.response:
I went to look at what DaVinci spotted in the treeline. Which, if you'd been standing there, you'd know.

Look, I hear you on the signal equipment and I'll get to it. But you don't get to be the only one who decides what the priority is in any given moment. DaVinci thought he saw something moving near the treeline. That's worth thirty seconds of attention before I go back to the checklist.

What did you actually need from me?

day_4.utterance: There's something I never told you all. Before we left, I told my family our flight path. They know roughly where we were headed. I just don't know if they'll call it in.
day_4.response:
They will. If you told them the flight path and you don't show up, they call it in. That's what people do. And the airline already knows the flight path — they filed it before we left the ground. Search and rescue isn't starting from zero here.

Why didn't you mention this earlier? That's actually useful information. Do you know roughly how specific you were — like, did you tell them a route, or just the destination? Because that affects how tight the search area is.

And honestly — why are you sitting on stuff like this? First the thing about Donatello, now this. You notice things and you know things and you go quiet instead of saying them out loud. I'm not mad, I just need you to understand that out here, the thing you almost didn't say is sometimes the thing that matters most.

day_4.utterance: If the information is accurate, rescue could arrive within 48 hours. We need to keep our current supplies intact until then.
day_4.response:
Yeah, that's right. 48 hours is manageable. We're not in crisis mode, we just need to not do anything stupid between now and then.

So here's what that actually means in practice. We don't launch the raft — not because the plan is bad, but because if rescue is coming to this location, we need to be at this location. We keep the signal running, we conserve water and food, we don't take unnecessary risks. DaVinci, that means the reef swim is off the table for now. I'm serious about that one.

Someone needs to get up and feed that fire.

day_4.utterance: Are you scared? …I am. Not of dying. I'm scared of just… disappearing without leaving anything behind.
day_4.response:
Yeah. I know that feeling.

I think about it differently though. The things you leave behind aren't necessarily the big obvious ones. It's more like — the fact that you noticed Donatello with the crackers and told me instead of just letting it go. The fact that you asked me what kind of people we'd become instead of just not thinking about it. The fact that you sat with that question instead of brushing it off. Those things matter. They changed how this played out.

I'm not going to tell you that you've left some massive mark on the world, because I don't know that and I'm not going to say something just because it sounds good. But I do think the fear of disappearing without mattering is one of those things that's a lot louder when you're scared and exhausted and sitting in the dark. It doesn't mean it's telling you the truth.

You're here. You're still here. That's not nothing.

Feed the fire and get some sleep. Forty-eight hours.

day_5.utterance: *Stands up, eyes red, looking at you and the others. His lips move, but nothing comes out.*
day_5.response:
Hey. Hey, it's okay. Breathe.

Someone get on that radio and tell them our position. Right now, before it cuts out.

day_5.utterance: These past few days… I know I haven't been easy to be around.
day_5.response:
You really haven't. But you kept us alive, so I'll take the trade.

Seriously though — the water runs, the rationing, the raft plan, the task log. That stuff mattered. I don't think any of us would have made it 48 hours without it. You just also made it harder than it needed to be sometimes, and I think you know that.

For what it's worth, the moment at the end when you said you were scared and taking it out on me instead — that was the most useful thing you said the whole time we were out here. Not because it fixed anything, but because it was honest and it cost you something to say it. That's the version of you I'd want around if this ever happened again.

Which it won't. Because we are getting on that rescue and I am never getting on a plane again.

day_5.utterance: *The three of them drift apart, each doing their own thing. No one takes charge. The silence settles over the camp.*
day_5.response:
Alright, three hours is enough time to do this right. We're not just walking away from this.

Donatello, tear out whatever pages you need from that notebook but leave the rationing plan and the task log — someone doing a post-incident review is going to want that information and it's more useful to them than to us once we're home.

DaVinci, before you finish packing — help me break down anything we built that someone else might be able to use if they end up out here. The fuselage windbreak stays because we didn't build that, but the signal pile, the water collection setup, any of the raft materials we didn't lash together — stack them somewhere visible and accessible.

Michelangelo, I know you're watching the sky and that's fine, but when you're ready I want you to write down the flight path information you gave your family — as much detail as you can remember. For the incident report. They're going to ask.

And somebody needs to make sure that fire is completely out before we leave. Last thing we need is to start a wildfire on top of everything else.

Three hours. Let's use them.

day_5.utterance: I dreamed about home last night.

day_5.response:
How much is there?

Look, I'm not going to relitigate the whole thing right now. We're three hours from rescue. But I want you to understand something — the emergency you were saving it for? This was it. Every day out here was the emergency. And the rest of us were rationing on the assumption that what we had was what we had.

What do you want to do with it? Because we can either eat it now, which honestly we probably should, or we leave it with the infrastructure for whoever ends up out here next. Those are the two options that make sense to me. What I don't want is for it to just sit there while nobody says anything.

day_5.utterance: I logged every resource and decision from these five days. I'm going to write it up as a proper report when we get back. On the last page I left myself a question I haven't answered yet — if you had to do it over, what would you change?
day_5.response:
Honestly? I'd push harder on communication earlier. Day one, I was already thinking in terms of priorities and logistics, but I was also kind of managing everyone individually instead of just putting everything on the table at once. The thing with you and the food — I should have addressed the group dynamics directly on day one instead of waiting for something to happen. By the time I brought it up, trust had already taken a hit.

The other thing is Michelangelo. I kept treating him like a problem to manage rather than a person with something to contribute. And it turned out the most useful piece of information we had — the flight path, his family knowing where we were headed — was sitting with him the whole time because nobody made him feel like saying it out loud was safe. That one's on me.

The stuff I'd keep — the decision to prioritize the signal over the raft, the water logic, confronting you directly instead of letting it fester. Those were right.

What's your answer? You wrote the question. You must have something.

day_5.utterance: First thing when I get back — I'm going to compile all the resource data from these five days into a report.
day_5.response:
That's actually worth doing. If you write it up properly — resource consumption rates, decision points, what worked and what didn't — that's genuinely useful information. Not just for you, but for anyone who ends up in a similar situation and wants to know what the actual numbers look like on day one versus day three.

Send me a copy when you're done. I'm serious. I want to read it.

And add a section on the human factors stuff. Not feelings, I know that's not your thing — but the decisions that got made because of morale, good and bad. The crackers, the rationing plan, Michelangelo sitting on the flight path information. That stuff is part of the data too, even if it doesn't fit cleanly into a spreadsheet. Especially because it doesn't.

day_5.utterance: Those flowers DaVinci drew on the beach… I never really understood what they were for. What practical purpose did they serve out here?
day_5.response:
None. They didn't serve a practical purpose.

But DaVinci needed to feel like a person out here, not just a survivor. And a person who still draws flowers next to an SOS sign when everything is falling apart is a person who hasn't given up. That mattered. You said yourself that morale was a resource and we had four days before people started breaking down. The flowers were part of why that didn't happen.

I'm an engineer. My instinct is to cut everything that doesn't have a function. But I've been wrong about that enough times that I've learned to at least ask the question before I cut it. Sometimes the thing that looks useless is holding something else together that you can't see.

Look at him right now. He's cheering. We need that guy to have stayed that guy. The flowers are part of why he did.

day_5.utterance: *His cheering stops. He looks over at you, notices you haven't moved, and the smile slowly fades. He waits.*
day_5.response:
I don't know why I'm not moving. I know what that is out there. I know what it means.

I think I just need a second to be in this. Because in about an hour this is over and we go back to being people with jobs and apartments and normal problems, and I haven't figured out yet how to feel about that.

Four days ago I didn't know any of you. Now I know that Donatello is scared underneath all the logistics, and that Michelangelo almost didn't say the thing that mattered most, and that you draw flowers when things are hard and you think nobody's watching. And that's going to be a weird thing to carry around.

I'm okay. I'm coming.

day_5.utterance: Rescue is here… they're waving us over. Are you going? I'll follow you.
